sentences.text: Multan, September 1949.
In the New Central Jail, a scholar finishes the preface to his book.
His name is Abul A'la Mawdudi.
The book is Tafhim al-Qur'an: making the Qur'an understood.
The preface is only nine pages.
But it holds a whole way of learning the Qur'an.
Here it is, in plain English.
He opens with an honest question.
So much translation and tafsir already existed in Urdu.
Why add one more?
A new translation made only for the blessing of it, he says, is no longer a good use of time.
It is worth doing only if it fills a gap: something earlier translators left, or a need of the Qur'an's students that earlier works did not meet.
And he had felt such a need for a long time.
Ordinary educated people wanted to reach the spirit of the Qur'an, and to know what this Book is really after.
The translators had done valuable work.
Yet that wish, he writes, was still thirsty.
He also felt that he could do something to quench that thirst.
Those two feelings started this book.
So who is it for?
Not scholars.
Not people trained in Arabic and the religious sciences.
Plenty already exists for them.
It is for people of ordinary education, who do not know Arabic well.
So he left out many debates that matter to specialists.
His aim was simple.
An ordinary reader should understand the meaning clearly, and feel the effect the Qur'an itself wants to have.
Where a confusion may arise, clear it.
Where a question comes to mind, answer it right there.
And he asks his readers, and the scholars, to tell him where he fell short.
This, he says, is not the last word.
Then comes the heart of the preface.
How do you bring the Qur'an into another language?
He chose a free, interpretive rendering.
He calls it tarjumani.
Not because word-for-word translation is wrong.
Great scholars had already done it well: Shah Waliullah in Persian, and in Urdu Shah Abdul Qadir, Shah Rafiuddin, Mawlana Mahmud al-Hasan, Mawlana Ashraf Ali, and Hafiz Fateh Muhammad Jalandhari.
A literal translation has a real benefit: you learn what every word means.
But for a reader who does not know Arabic, he says, it has several weaknesses.
The first is life.
Under the lines of the Qur'an, the reader finds lifeless text.
His soul is not stirred.
His hair does not stand on end.
No tears come.
No storm rises inside him.
He may even wonder: is this really the Book that challenged the whole world to bring anything like it?
A literal translation, he says, is a sieve.
Only the dry ingredients of the medicine pass through.
The living spirit of the language flies off above it.
Yet the Qur'an's power came as much from its language as from its teaching.
That is what melted hearts of stone, and shook Arabia like lightning.
Its fiercest enemies feared that whoever listened would lose his heart to it.
Had it come in the language of its translations, he says, it could never have done that.
Another weakness is flow.
Translations sit between the lines, or on half a page.
Good for study, but you cannot read them straight through like a book.
English is worse: every verse cut out and numbered, in the style of Bible translations.
Take any fine essay, he says, and number its sentences.
Half of its effect is gone.
Another reason, and he calls it a very important one: the Qur'an is speech, not writing.
It did not come as written booklets.
As the call to Islam moved forward, an address was revealed to the Prophet, peace be upon him, for each occasion, and he delivered it to people like a sermon.
Speech works differently.
On paper, you first state an objection, then answer it.
In a speech the objectors are standing right there, so the speaker simply answers.
On paper, words must explain the setting.
In speech, the setting is all around.
And in speech the voices shift.
A group is spoken about, then spoken to.
One person, then many.
Sometimes the speaker speaks for himself, sometimes for a group, sometimes for a higher power, and sometimes that higher power itself speaks.
Heard aloud, this is beauty.
On paper, it can feel disconnected.
In Arabic, only notes can help, because not a letter of the text may change.
But in another language, if speech is carefully turned into written style, the gap closes.
Beyond that, every surah was an address for a particular moment.
It had a background, and needs it came to meet.
Strip that away, and a bare translation leaves some things not understood, some understood upside down.
A rendering can carry some of that background with it.
And then there is vocabulary.
The Qur'an has its own language within the language.
Take one word: kufr.
In one place it means complete disbelief.
In another, simple denial.
In another, only ingratitude.
In another, falling short in something faith requires.
In another, believing in principle but refusing in practice.
In another, obeying outwardly while disbelieving inside.
Translate it as kufr everywhere, and you are technically correct.
Yet the reader will miss the meaning here, misread it there, and be lost somewhere else.
So here is what he did.
He did not dress the Qur'an's words in Urdu clothes.
He read a passage, took the meaning he understood and the effect it left on his heart, and carried that, as faithfully as he could, into his own language.
Clear Arabic should become clear Urdu.
The flow of speech should come through naturally.
And the majesty and force of God's Word should show, as far as possible.
That needed freedom.
But this was the Word of God.
So, he writes: I used this freedom while very much afraid.
And he took care never to go beyond what the Qur'an's own words allow.
What a rendering cannot carry, two more tools fill.
Before every surah, an introduction: when it was revealed, what was happening, what stage the movement of Islam had reached, what needs and problems it faced.
And notes, written in only two kinds of places.
Where an ordinary reader would want an explanation, or a doubt would rise.
And where a reader might hurry past, and miss the real spirit of a verse.
Nothing that pulls the eye away from the Qur'an.
Then he gives the reader a method.
One: read the surah's introduction carefully, and return to it while you study that surah.
Two: take the portion you read each day, and first go through a word-for-word translation, verse by verse.
Persian, Urdu or English, whichever you like.
Three: read his rendering of that portion straight through, without the notes, so the whole message stands before you at once.
Four: go back, verse by verse, with the notes, for the detail.
Read like this, he says, and an ordinary reader will come to know the Qur'an well.
Perhaps not like a scholar.
But well, in sha' Allah.
And the book itself?
He began in February 1942.
For more than five years he worked, until he reached the end of Surah Yusuf.
Then one thing after another left him no time to write, or even to revise.
Call it good luck or bad luck, he writes.
In October 1948 he was suddenly arrested and sent to jail.
And there, he found the time the book needed.
He ends with a prayer: that it truly helps God's servants understand the Qur'an.
And a line in Arabic.
Wa ma tawfiqi illa billah.
My success is only through God.
Read the setting.
Learn the words.
Hear it whole.
Then go deep.
